goals: Label a tooth and state the function of each type of tooth
Write the adult dental formula and use it to count teeth
Name the organs of the alimentary canal and the digestive glands with their secretions

slides.heading: Teeth and the Digestive System
slides.body_md: Part 1 — how food is cut, ground and moved along, and which glands help.

visual.alt: Flow from teeth to the alimentary canal to the digestive glands

slides.narration: Food is of no use to the body until it is made small and soluble. The teeth begin the job by cutting and grinding. The alimentary canal then carries the food along while glands pour in juices that digest it.

slides.heading: Structure of a tooth
slides.body_md: Three regions: the **crown** above the gum, the **neck** at the gum and the **root** in the jaw bone.

slides.narration: A tooth has a crown that shows above the gum, a neck at the gum line and a root fixed in the jaw bone. The crown is covered by enamel. Inside lies dentine, and at the centre is the pulp cavity with blood vessels and nerves.

slides.heading: Parts of a tooth and what they do

rows: Hardest substance in the body; covers the crown
Protects the tooth from wear and acid
Bone-like, yellowish; forms most of the tooth
Gives the tooth its shape and strength
Brings food and oxygen; gives the sense of pain and temperature
Thin bony layer round the root
Fixes the root in the jaw bone
Holds the tooth firmly and protects the root

visual.alt: Table of the parts of a tooth with their description and function

slides.narration: Enamel is the hardest part and protects the crown. Dentine forms most of the tooth. The pulp cavity holds blood vessels and nerves, which is why a decayed tooth that reaches it hurts. Cement fixes the root in the jaw, and the gum holds the neck.

slides.heading: Four types of teeth

visual.alt: Table of the four types of teeth with shape, number and function

slides.narration: The four types of teeth suit four jobs. Incisors cut and bite. Canines tear. Premolars and molars have broad tops with bumps, and they crush and grind the food into a paste that is easy to swallow.

slides.heading: Quick check: the tearing tooth
slides.body_md: Which type of tooth is pointed and used for tearing food?
slides.narration: Think of the long pointed tooth next to the incisors.

slides.heading: The dental formula of an adult
slides.body_md: For **one half** of each jaw: incisors, canines, premolars, molars.

visual.alt: Table giving two, one, two and three teeth for each type in the upper and lower half jaw

slides.narration: The dental formula shows the teeth in one half of the upper jaw and one half of the lower jaw. In an adult it reads two, one, two, three above and two, one, two, three below. Each half jaw has eight teeth.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting all the teeth
slides.body_md: Use the dental formula to find the teeth of each type and the total in an adult mouth.
bullets: Step 1: a mouth has 4 half jaws (2 upper, 2 lower).
Step 2: incisors 2 × 4 = **8**; canines 1 × 4 = **4**; premolars 2 × 4 = **8**; molars 3 × 4 = **12**.
Step 3: total = 8 + 4 + 8 + 12 = **32**; one jaw has **16**.

visual.alt: Worked table: eight incisors, four canines, eight premolars, twelve molars and thirty-two teeth in all

slides.narration: There are four half jaws, so multiply each number in the formula by four. That gives eight incisors, four canines, eight premolars and twelve molars. Together they make thirty-two teeth, sixteen in each jaw.

slides.heading: The human digestive system
slides.body_md: The **alimentary canal** is one long tube from mouth to anus; the **glands** lie beside it.

slides.narration: The alimentary canal begins at the mouth and runs through the oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine to the anus. The salivary glands, liver and pancreas lie outside the tube but pour their juices into it through ducts.

slides.heading: Organs of the alimentary canal

rows: Teeth chew; saliva wets the food and starts starch digestion
Pushes food down by waves of contraction
Churns food; gastric juice starts protein digestion
Digestion is completed and food is absorbed

visual.alt: Table of the organs of the alimentary canal and what happens in each

slides.narration: In the mouth food is chewed and mixed with saliva. The oesophagus pushes it to the stomach, where it is churned. Digestion ends and absorption happens in the small intestine. The large intestine absorbs water, and the rest leaves through the anus.

slides.heading: Quick check: not part of the canal
slides.body_md: Which of these is a digestive gland and not part of the alimentary canal?
slides.narration: The food never passes through it.

slides.heading: The digestive glands

visual.alt: Table of five digestive glands with their secretions and where each is poured

slides.narration: There are five sets of digestive glands. Salivary glands give saliva to the mouth. Gastric glands give gastric juice to the stomach. The liver gives bile and the pancreas gives pancreatic juice, both to the duodenum. Intestinal glands give intestinal juice.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: teeth lost in an accident
slides.body_md: A patient lost all four canines and all eight premolars. How many teeth are left, and can he still grind food?
bullets: Step 1: teeth lost = 4 + 8 = **12**.
Step 2: teeth left = 32 − 12 = **20**.
Step 3: 12 molars remain, so he can still **grind**, but he will find it hard to **tear** tough food.

visual.alt: Worked table: thirty-two teeth before, twelve lost, twenty left

slides.narration: Add the canines and premolars lost to get twelve. Subtract from thirty-two to leave twenty teeth. The incisors and molars are still there, so cutting and grinding are possible, but tearing is poor because the canines are gone.

slides.heading: Quick check: bile
slides.narration: It is stored in the gall bladder but made elsewhere.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: A tooth: enamel, dentine, pulp cavity, cement; crown, neck, root.
Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars and molars grind; adult formula gives thirty-two teeth.
The alimentary canal is a tube; the salivary glands, liver and pancreas pour juices into it.

visual.alt: Summary table of the types of teeth and their functions

slides.narration: To recap. Enamel covers the crown and the pulp cavity holds the nerves. Incisors cut, canines tear, and premolars and molars grind. An adult has thirty-two teeth. Food passes along the alimentary canal while five sets of glands add their juices.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: In a tooth diagram, show **enamel, dentine, pulp cavity, cement** and the **gum**, with **crown, neck, root**.
Write the formula for **one half** of each jaw, then double it to get **32**.
Say the **liver makes bile** and the **gall bladder stores** it.
Name each gland with its **secretion**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Draw the tooth with all its layers and name crown, neck and root. Write the dental formula for one half of each jaw and double it. Remember the liver makes bile and the gall bladder only stores it. Always name a gland together with its secretion.

decks.title: Teeth and the Digestive System — Part 2: Digestive enzymes, absorption and assimilation
goals: Tabulate the enzymes, substrates and end products in the mouth, stomach and small intestine
Explain how villi are adapted for absorption
Describe how absorbed nutrients are carried and assimilated

slides.heading: Enzymes, Absorption and Assimilation
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how large food molecules become small ones, and where they go next.

visual.alt: Flow from large molecules through enzymes to small molecules and then to blood and lymph

slides.narration: Starch, protein and fat are too large to pass into the blood. Enzymes break them into small soluble molecules. These are then absorbed into the blood and lymph and carried to every cell of the body.

slides.heading: In the mouth
slides.body_md: Saliva is slightly alkaline and also contains mucus, which makes the food slippery. Chewing for a long time lets more starch change to maltose.

visual.alt: Table of the digestive enzyme in the mouth with its substrate and end product

slides.narration: In the mouth, saliva wets the food. It holds an enzyme called salivary amylase, which changes some starch into maltose, a sugar. That is why a piece of rice or bread tastes a little sweeter if you chew it for long.

slides.heading: In the stomach

rows: Makes the stomach acidic, kills germs and helps pepsin work
Curdles milk so that it stays longer in the stomach
Coats the stomach wall and protects it from acid

visual.alt: Table of the parts of gastric juice and what each does

slides.narration: Gastric juice has hydrochloric acid, the enzyme pepsin and mucus. The acid kills germs and gives pepsin the acidic conditions it needs. Pepsin starts to break protein into peptones. Mucus protects the stomach wall from the acid.

slides.heading: Quick check: the protein enzyme of the stomach
slides.body_md: Which enzyme begins the digestion of protein in the stomach?
slides.narration: Think of the acid in the stomach.

slides.heading: In the small intestine

rows: No enzyme; makes the food alkaline and breaks fat into tiny droplets (emulsification)
Maltase, sucrase, lactase (sugars), erepsin (peptides to amino acids), lipase

visual.alt: Table of bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice with their sources and actions

slides.narration: Bile has no enzymes. It makes the food alkaline and breaks large fat drops into tiny droplets. Pancreatic juice has enzymes for starch, protein and fat. Intestinal juice completes the job by turning sugars into simple sugars and peptides into amino acids.

slides.heading: The master table of digestion

visual.alt: Master table of digestive enzymes by region with substrate and end product

slides.narration: This table is worth learning by heart. In the mouth, amylase gives maltose. In the stomach, pepsin gives peptones. In the small intestine, amylase, trypsin and lipase continue the work, and maltase, sucrase, lactase and erepsin finish it, giving glucose, amino acids, fatty acids and glycerol.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: following starch through the canal
slides.body_md: A mouthful of boiled rice is mostly starch. Trace what happens to its starch until it can be absorbed.
bullets: Step 1: **mouth**: salivary amylase changes some starch to maltose.
Step 2: **stomach**: no starch digestion; the acid stops salivary amylase.
Step 3: **small intestine**: pancreatic amylase changes the rest of the starch to maltose.
Step 4: **small intestine**: maltase changes maltose to **glucose**, which is absorbed.

visual.alt: Flow showing starch changing to maltose by amylase and maltose changing to glucose by maltase

slides.narration: Follow the starch. Salivary amylase changes some of it to maltose in the mouth. The acid in the stomach stops that enzyme. In the small intestine pancreatic amylase changes the rest to maltose, and maltase then changes maltose to glucose, which is absorbed.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reading an enzyme experiment
slides.body_md: Saliva was added to starch solution in two tubes. A was kept at 37 degrees and B at 10 degrees. Starch disappeared (no blue-black colour with iodine) after 6 minutes in A and 24 minutes in B. What do the results show?
bullets: Step 1: B took 24 ÷ 6 = **4** times as long.
Step 2: the enzyme in saliva works **faster at body temperature** than at a low temperature.
Step 3: the starch was changed to sugar, which does not give the blue-black colour with iodine.

visual.alt: Worked table of the two tubes with temperature and time for starch to disappear

slides.narration: Compare the two times. The cold tube took four times as long as the warm one. Salivary amylase works best at about body temperature, and it is slowed down when it is cold. The starch is turned into sugar, so the iodine test turns negative.

slides.heading: Quick check: end products of fat digestion
slides.body_md: The end products of the digestion of fats are
slides.narration: Lipase breaks fat into two kinds of molecule.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: what villi add to the surface
slides.body_md: A patch of intestine wall is 5 mm by 4 mm. There are 25 villi on every square millimetre, and each adds 0.4 square millimetre of surface. Find the villi and the gain in surface.
bullets: Step 1: flat area = 5 × 4 = **20** square millimetres.

sections.heading: 1. Structure of a tooth; types of teeth; dental formula
sections.body_md:
A tooth has three regions: the **crown** (above the gum), the **neck** (at the gum) and the **root** (in a socket of the jaw bone).

| Part | Description | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Enamel** | Hardest substance in the body; covers the crown | Protects against wear and acid |
| **Dentine** | Bone-like, yellowish; most of the tooth | Shape and strength |
| **Pulp cavity** | Soft; blood vessels and nerves | Nourishes the tooth; gives the sense of pain |
| **Cement** | Thin bony layer round the root | Fixes the root in the jaw bone |
| **Gum** | Soft tissue round the neck | Holds the tooth and protects the root |

| Type | Function |
|---|---|
| **Incisors** | Cutting and biting |
| **Canines** | Tearing and piercing |
| **Premolars** | Crushing and grinding |
| **Molars** | Grinding food finely |

**Dental formula of an adult** (one half of each jaw): incisors 2, canines 1, premolars 2, molars 3 above, and the same below. Each half jaw has 8 teeth, each jaw 16 and the whole mouth **32** teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars.

The four last molars (third molars, or wisdom teeth) appear late and some adults never grow them, so a mouth can have 28 teeth.

sections.heading: 2. The alimentary canal and the digestive glands
sections.body_md:
The **alimentary canal** is a long muscular tube from the **mouth** to the **anus**: mouth (buccal cavity), pharynx, **oesophagus**, **stomach**, **small intestine** (duodenum, jejunum, ileum), **large intestine** (colon and rectum) and **anus**. Food passes through it; digestion and absorption take place along it.

| Gland | Secretion | Poured into |
|---|---|---|
| **Salivary glands** | Saliva | Mouth |
| **Gastric glands** (in the stomach wall) | Gastric juice | Stomach |
| **Liver** | Bile (stored in the **gall bladder**) | Duodenum |
| **Pancreas** | Pancreatic juice | Duodenum |
| **Intestinal glands** (in the wall of the small intestine) | Intestinal juice | Small intestine |

The **liver**, **gall bladder** and **pancreas** are *accessory organs*: food never passes through them. The liver is the largest gland in the body.

The first part of the small intestine, where bile and pancreatic juice enter.

sections.heading: 3. Digestive enzymes and their action
sections.body_md:
**Digestion** changes large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones with the help of **enzymes**.

| Region | Enzyme | Substrate | End product |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mouth | Salivary amylase | Starch | Maltose |
| Stomach | **Pepsin** (with HCl) | Protein | Peptones |
| Stomach | Rennin (infants) | Milk protein | Curd |
| Small intestine | Pancreatic amylase | Starch | Maltose |
| Small intestine | Trypsin | Proteins, peptones | Peptides, amino acids |
| Small intestine | Lipase | Emulsified fats | Fatty acids and glycerol |
| Small intestine | Maltase | Maltose | Glucose |
| Small intestine | Sucrase | Sucrose | Glucose and fructose |
| Small intestine | Lactase | Lactose | Glucose and galactose |
| Small intestine | Erepsin | Peptides | Amino acids |

**Bile** contains no enzyme. It makes the food alkaline and **emulsifies** fats (breaks big drops into tiny droplets), giving lipase a larger surface to act on. **Hydrochloric acid** in gastric juice kills germs and gives the acid medium for pepsin. Mucus protects the stomach wall.

Books differ slightly in the names and the list of enzymes; this chapter follows the common ICSE list.

Breaking a fat into tiny droplets by bile.

sections.heading: 4. Absorption and assimilation
sections.body_md:
**Absorption** is the passage of digested food through the wall of the small intestine into the blood or lymph. Most absorption takes place in the **small intestine**; the large intestine absorbs mainly water.

**Villi** are finger-like projections of the wall of the small intestine. Adaptations: millions of villi give a **large surface**; the wall is **one cell thick**; a dense network of **capillaries** carries away glucose and amino acids; a central **lacteal** takes up fatty acids and glycerol; muscle fibres move the villi.

- **Glucose and amino acids** go into capillaries, then by the **hepatic portal vein** to the **liver**.
- **Fatty acids and glycerol** go into the lacteals (lymph) and reach the blood later.

**Assimilation** is the use of absorbed food by cells.
- Glucose gives **energy**; extra is stored as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles.
- Amino acids build **proteins** for growth and repair.
- Fats form **cell membranes** and are stored as fat under the skin and round organs; fat is also a source of energy.
- Undigested food is passed out as **faeces**.

A finger-like projection of the small intestine wall that absorbs food.
The use of absorbed food by the cells for energy, growth and repair.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing the dental formula for the **whole mouth** and forgetting that it is given for **half** of each jaw.
- Calling **bile** an enzyme, or saying the **gall bladder makes** bile.
- Naming only the enzyme and leaving out the **substrate** or the **end product**.
- Sending **fats into capillaries**; they go into the **lacteal**.
- Leaving out the **gum** or the **pulp cavity** in a tooth diagram.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two functions or two points, matched.
- 3 marks: a three-row comparison or three enzymes with substrate and end product.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Canines are the teeth used mainly for cutting vegetables into thin slices.
questions.solution_md: False. Incisors cut and bite; canines tear.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the way of writing the number of each type of tooth in one half of the upper and lower jaw.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dental formula.**

questions.solution_md: Dental formula.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Incisor, Canine, Gum, Molar.

answer.model_answer_md: **Gum**; the others are **types of teeth**.

questions.solution_md: The gum is soft tissue, not a tooth.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: molars have broad tops with bumps.

answer.model_answer_md: They are meant for **grinding** food into a paste, and a broad bumpy surface grinds better.

questions.solution_md: For grinding.

questions.stem_md: Two molars are lost from each half jaw in an accident. How many teeth are left in an adult mouth that had the full set of 32?
questions.solution_md: Teeth lost = 2 × 4 = 8; left = 32 − 8 = 24.

questions.stem_md: An adult never grew the 4 third molars (wisdom teeth). How many molars does the person have in all?
questions.solution_md: An adult normally has 12 molars; 12 − 4 = 8.

questions.stem_md: Name the part of a tooth that (i) covers the crown and (ii) holds the blood vessels and nerves.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Enamel**, the hardest substance in the body, covers the crown of the tooth. (ii) The **pulp cavity**, at the centre of the tooth, holds the blood vessels and nerves.

questions.solution_md: Enamel; pulp cavity.

questions.stem_md: State one function each of (i) incisors and (ii) premolars.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Incisors** have a flat, sharp edge and are used to cut and bite food. (ii) **Premolars** have broad tops with two bumps and are used to crush and grind food.

questions.solution_md: Incisors cut; premolars grind.

questions.stem_md: Write the dental formula of an adult for one half of each jaw and state the total number of teeth in the mouth.

answer.model_answer_md: Incisors **2**, canines **1**, premolars **2**, molars **3** in each half jaw, upper and lower alike. Each half jaw has 8 teeth, so the mouth has 8 × 4 = **32** teeth.

questions.solution_md: Formula 2, 1, 2, 3; 32 teeth.

questions.solution_md: Cement; dentine; enamel.

questions.stem_md: Starch solution was mixed with saliva and kept warm. After some minutes a drop of the mixture no longer turned blue-black with iodine. This shows that the saliva had

options.text_md: changed the starch into a sugar

questions.solution_md: Salivary amylase changed starch into maltose, which gives no blue-black colour — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Cubes of boiled egg white (a protein) are kept at body temperature in four test tubes, each with pepsin. In which tube will the egg white be digested?

options.text_md: The tube to which an alkali has been added
The tube to which dilute hydrochloric acid has been added
The tube to which oil has been added
The tube to which nothing else has been added

questions.solution_md: Pepsin works in an acid medium, which the dilute acid provides — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A patient's bile duct is blocked, so bile cannot reach the duodenum. Digestion that will be affected most is that of
questions.solution_md: Bile emulsifies fats, so lipase cannot work well without it — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The enzyme trypsin, in pancreatic juice, acts on
questions.solution_md: Trypsin digests proteins and peptones to peptides and amino acids — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A baby cannot digest the sugar in milk because the enzyme that acts on it is missing. The enzyme and the sugar are
questions.solution_md: Lactase breaks lactose into glucose and galactose — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Pepsin acts on protein in the stomach.

**Reason (R):** Gastric juice contains hydrochloric acid, which gives the acid medium that pepsin needs.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the acid explains why pepsin works in the stomach — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Bile helps in the digestion of fats.

**Reason (R):** Bile contains the enzyme lipase.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: bile has no enzyme; it emulsifies fats — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Hydrochloric acid in gastric juice is an enzyme that digests protein.
questions.solution_md: False. The acid is not an enzyme; pepsin is the enzyme, and the acid gives it the right medium.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Bile contains the enzyme lipase.
questions.solution_md: False. Bile has no enzyme; lipase is in pancreatic and intestinal juice.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the breaking of large fat drops into tiny droplets by bile.

answer.model_answer_md: **Emulsification.**

questions.solution_md: Emulsification.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Pepsin, Trypsin, Bile, Lipase.

answer.model_answer_md: **Bile**; the others are **enzymes**.

questions.solution_md: Bile has no enzyme.

questions.stem_md: Saliva was added to starch in tube P at 37 degrees and in tube Q at 20 degrees. The starch had gone after 8 minutes in P and 16 minutes in Q. How many minutes longer did Q take?
questions.solution_md: 16 − 8 = 8 minutes.

questions.stem_md:
Select the correct terms to fill in the blanks: [pepsin, bile, saliva, lacteal, maltose, glycogen, pancreas, villi]

The amylase of (a) ______ changes starch into (b) ______. The enzyme (c) ______ begins the digestion of protein in the stomach. Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the (d) ______ of a villus. Extra glucose is stored in the liver as (e) ______.
questions.solution_md: (a) saliva; (b) maltose; (c) pepsin; (d) lacteal; (e) glycogen.

questions.stem_md: State two functions of hydrochloric acid in gastric juice.

answer.model_answer_md: The acid **kills germs** that enter the stomach with the food. It also gives the **acid medium** in which the enzyme pepsin works best.

questions.solution_md: Kills germs; acid medium for pepsin.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which bile helps in digestion.

answer.model_answer_md: Bile **emulsifies fats**, breaking big drops into tiny droplets, and makes the food **alkaline** for the enzymes of the small intestine.

questions.solution_md: Emulsifies fats; makes the food alkaline.

questions.stem_md: Name the enzyme in saliva and state its substrate and end product.

answer.model_answer_md: The enzyme in saliva is **salivary amylase**. Its substrate is **starch**, which it changes into the sugar **maltose** in the mouth.

questions.solution_md: Salivary amylase; starch; maltose.

questions.stem_md: Why does the stomach wall not get digested by the pepsin and acid in gastric juice?

answer.model_answer_md: A layer of **mucus**, made by cells of the stomach wall, **coats** it and **protects** it from the acid and pepsin.

questions.solution_md: Mucus coats and protects.

marking_scheme.step: Protects it from acid and pepsin

questions.stem_md: Tabulate the enzyme, substrate and end product of digestion in (i) the mouth, (ii) the stomach and (iii) the small intestine for fats.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Region | Enzyme | Substrate | End product |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mouth | **Salivary amylase** | **Starch** | **Maltose** |
| Stomach | **Pepsin** | **Protein** | **Peptones** |
| Small intestine | **Lipase** | **Emulsified fats** | **Fatty acids and glycerol** |

questions.solution_md: Amylase; pepsin; lipase, each with substrate and product.

questions.stem_md: Name the three enzymes of pancreatic juice and state the food that each acts on.

answer.model_answer_md: **Amylase** acts on **starch** and forms maltose. **Trypsin** acts on **proteins** and **peptones** and forms peptides and amino acids. **Lipase** acts on emulsified **fats** and forms fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.solution_md: Amylase: starch; trypsin: protein; lipase: fat.

questions.stem_md: Glucose absorbed in the small intestine is carried by the hepatic portal vein first to the
questions.solution_md: The hepatic portal vein carries absorbed food to the liver — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which feature of a villus helps digested food pass quickly into the blood?

options.text_md: Its wall is only one cell thick
Its surface is covered by thick mucus only

questions.solution_md: A very thin wall gives a short path for the food — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A patient has a short length of small intestine removed and loses weight because less food is absorbed. This is mainly because the

options.text_md: surface area with villi is reduced

questions.solution_md: Fewer villi mean less surface for absorption — option (c).

questions.stem_md: In the figure of a villus, which letter marks the tube that takes up fatty acids and glycerol?
questions.solution_md: C is the lacteal; A is the epithelium, B the capillary network, D an intestinal gland and E the muscle layer — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Most of the digested food is absorbed in the small intestine.

**Reason (R):** The large intestine absorbs water from the undigested food.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the second statement does not explain the first — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Fatty acids and glycerol are absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi.
questions.solution_md: False. They are absorbed into the lacteals; glucose and amino acids go into the capillaries.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Villi are found on the inner wall of the small intestine.
questions.solution_md: True.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the use of absorbed food by the cells of the body for energy, growth and repair.

answer.model_answer_md: **Assimilation.**

questions.solution_md: Assimilation.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the inner wall of the small intestine is folded into villi.

answer.model_answer_md: Villi give a very **large surface area** for absorbing the digested food.

questions.solution_md: Large surface area.

questions.stem_md: A patch of the small intestine wall is 5 mm by 4 mm and has 25 villi on every square millimetre. How many villi are on the patch?
questions.solution_md: Area = 5 × 4 = 20 square millimetres; villi = 20 × 25 = 500.

questions.stem_md: A flat patch of intestine wall has an area of 20 square millimetres. With villi its total absorbing area is 220 square millimetres. How many times larger is the area with villi?
Name the vessel in a villus that carries away (i) glucose and (ii) fatty acids.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Glucose is carried away by the **blood capillaries**. (ii) Fatty acids are taken up by the **lacteal**.

questions.solution_md: Capillary; lacteal.

questions.stem_md: State the fate of (i) extra glucose and (ii) amino acids after absorption.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Extra glucose is stored as **glycogen** in the liver and muscles. (ii) Amino acids are used to build **proteins** for growth and repair.

questions.solution_md: Glycogen; proteins.

questions.stem_md: State three ways in which villi are adapted for absorption.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Millions of villi give a **large surface area**.
2. Their wall is **one cell thick**, so food passes quickly.
3. A network of **capillaries** and a **lacteal** carry the absorbed food away.

questions.solution_md: Surface; thin wall; capillaries and lacteal.

questions.stem_md: State what happens to the absorbed (i) glucose, (ii) amino acids and (iii) fatty acids and glycerol in the body.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Glucose** is oxidised for **energy**, and extra is stored as glycogen. (ii) **Amino acids** build **proteins** for growth and repair. (iii) **Fatty acids and glycerol** are used for energy, for making **cell membranes** or stored as **fat**.

questions.solution_md: Energy and glycogen; proteins; energy, membranes or stored fat.

Study the diagram of a tooth in section. Parts are lettered A to E.

(a) Name the parts A, B and C. [3]

(b) State one function each of the parts A and C. [2]

(c) The tooth in the figure is a molar. Write how many molars an adult has in one half of the upper jaw and in the whole mouth, and show how the dental formula gives 32 teeth in all. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of the human alimentary canal, naming six parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A is the **enamel**, B is the **dentine** and C is the **pulp cavity**.

**(b)** **Enamel** protects the crown from wear and acid. The **pulp cavity** holds the blood vessels and nerves that nourish the tooth and give the sense of pain.

**(c)** **3** molars in one half of the upper jaw and **12** in the whole mouth. Teeth in one half jaw = 2 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8; there are 4 half jaws, so 8 × 4 = **32**.

**(d)** A tube from the **mouth** through the **oesophagus**, **stomach**, **small intestine** and **large intestine** to the **anus**; six labels.

questions.solution_md: Enamel, dentine, pulp cavity; functions; 3 and 12, 32 teeth; labelled alimentary canal.

questions.stem_md:
Four test tubes each hold 5 mL of starch solution. Tube P has 2 mL of saliva at 37 degrees, tube Q has 2 mL of saliva at 20 degrees, tube R has 2 mL of boiled and cooled saliva at 37 degrees and tube S has 2 mL of water at 37 degrees. A drop from each tube is tested with iodine every 2 minutes. The starch has gone from P after 8 minutes and from Q after 16 minutes. R and S still give a blue-black colour after 60 minutes.

(a) Explain why tubes R and S still give a blue-black colour. [2]

(b) Calculate how many times longer Q took than P and give the reason. [2]

(c) Name the enzyme in saliva and the sugar formed from starch. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of tube P with the drop being tested on a tile, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** In **R** the enzyme was **destroyed by boiling**, and in **S** there was **no enzyme** at all, so the starch was not changed.

**(b)** 16 ÷ 8 = **2 times** longer. The enzyme works **more slowly at a lower temperature**; 37 degrees is close to body temperature.

**(c)** **Salivary amylase**; the sugar is **maltose**.

**(d)** A **test tube** holding **starch and saliva**, a **dropper** and a **tile with a drop of iodine**; four labels.

questions.solution_md: R boiled, S no enzyme; 2 times slower in the cold; amylase, maltose; labelled set-up.

questions.stem_md:
A patch of the wall of the small intestine is 6 mm by 5 mm. There are 20 villi on each square millimetre and each villus adds 0.4 square millimetre of surface.

(a) Calculate the number of villi on the patch. [2]

(b) Calculate the total absorbing area of the patch and how many times larger it is than the flat area. [3]

(c) State why the wall of a villus is only one cell thick. [1]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a villus, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Flat area = 6 × 5 = 30 square millimetres; villi = 30 × 20 = **600**.

**(b)** Extra area = 600 × 0.4 = 240; total = 30 + 240 = **270 square millimetres**, which is 270 ÷ 30 = **9 times** the flat area.

**(c)** A **thin wall** gives the digested food a **short path** to pass through quickly into the blood or lymph.

**(d)** A **finger-shaped villus** with **epithelium**, a **capillary network**, a **lacteal** and the **intestinal wall** below; four labels.

questions.solution_md: 600 villi; 270 square millimetres, 9 times; thin wall gives a short path; labelled villus.

marking_scheme.step: Thin wall gives a short path

questions.stem_md:
Ravi eats a meal of boiled rice, dal and a little butter.

(a) Name the type of teeth that bite off a piece of food and the type that grind the rice. [2]

(b) Name the enzyme in his mouth that acts on the rice and the sugar that it forms. [2]

(c) Name the enzyme that begins the digestion of the dal in the stomach and the medium it needs. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a tooth in section, naming four parts. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Incisors** bite off a piece; **molars** (and premolars) grind the rice.

**(b)** **Salivary amylase**; it forms **maltose** from starch.

**(c)** **Pepsin** begins protein digestion; it needs an **acidic** medium, provided by **hydrochloric acid**.

**(d)** A tooth with **crown, neck and root**, an **enamel** cap, **dentine**, a central **pulp cavity** and **cement** round the root, with four labels.

questions.solution_md: Incisors, molars; amylase, maltose; pepsin, acid; labelled tooth.

questions.stem_md:
A man has had his gall bladder removed. His liver and pancreas work normally. His doctor tells him to avoid very oily food.

(a) Name the juice that was stored in the gall bladder and the organ that makes it. [2]

(b) Explain why very oily food would cause the man discomfort. [2]

(c) Name the juice from another gland that also digests fats, the enzyme in it and the end products. [3]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a villus of the small intestine, naming three parts. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Bile**, made by the **liver**.

**(b)** Without the gall bladder, bile is not **stored and released in a large amount** when a heavy fatty meal arrives, so the fat is **not emulsified well** and **lipase** cannot digest it fully; the fat stays undigested and causes discomfort.

**(c)** **Pancreatic juice** from the pancreas; the enzyme is **lipase**; the end products are **fatty acids and glycerol**.

**(d)** A **finger-shaped villus** with its **epithelium**, **capillary network** and **lacteal**; three labels.

questions.solution_md: Bile, liver; less emulsification; pancreatic juice, lipase, fatty acids and glycerol; labelled diagram.

marking_scheme.step: Bile not stored or released in quantity
Fat not emulsified so lipase acts poorly
